unit.title: Business quality and macro
unit.description: Competitive advantages, the cycle, interest rates, macro data and how to analyse a company

steps.title: The five moats
steps.body:
Without an advantage to protect it, the competition ends up eating away the profits. Buffett calls it a **moat**:

1. **Intangible assets:** brands, patents, licences.
2. **Switching costs:** changing supplier is very costly.
3. **Network effect:** more users, more value.
4. **Cost advantage:** it produces more cheaply than anyone else.
5. **Efficient scale:** the market only has room for one or two players.

steps.title: How it shows up in the numbers
steps.body:
• **High, stable** margins and ROIC for 10 years.
• It can **raise prices** without losing customers, even with inflation.
• It holds on to or gains **market share**.

steps.title: A moat isn't a price
steps.body: In 2000, Microsoft and Cisco traded on P/Es of 60-100. Anyone who bought Microsoft at its 2000 peak took about **16 years** to get back to that price, even though the business remained excellent.
steps.key: A good business needs a moat; a good investment also needs a good price.

steps.title: The economic cycle
steps.body:
1. **Recovery:** low interest rates, the economy starts to grow.
2. **Expansion:** high employment and rising profits; inflation may appear.
3. **Slowdown:** rates go up and growth slows.
4. **Recession:** GDP falls (technically, two quarters in a row) and unemployment rises.

steps.title: Cyclical and defensive
steps.body:
**Cyclical:** cars, luxury goods, travel, industry, materials, banking, technology. They rise more in expansions and fall more in recessions.

**Defensive:** food, household and personal care, healthcare, utilities, water. People keep buying them in a crisis: they fall less and rise less.

steps.title: The stock market gets there first
steps.body: The stock market usually falls **before** a recession and rises **before** it ends. In March 2009 and March 2020 it hit bottom while the news was still terrible.
steps.key: The stock market doesn't look at the present: it looks at what it expects 6 or 12 months ahead.

steps.title: The price of money
steps.body:
• **ECB:** inflation target of **2 %** over the medium term.
• **Federal Reserve:** stable prices and maximum employment.

The ECB's benchmark rate is the **deposit facility rate**: in June 2026 it raised it to **2.25 %**. Check the current figure at ecb.europa.eu, because it changes several times a year.

steps.title: When rates go up
steps.body:
1. Loans and mortgages get more expensive.
2. People spend and invest less.
3. The economy cools and inflation falls (with a 12-24 month lag).
4. Savings accounts and bonds pay more: more competition for shares.
5. Future profits are worth less today: they're discounted at a higher rate.

steps.title: Who suffers most
steps.body: Growth companies with no profits, heavily indebted companies, property companies and **long-dated bonds**. In 2022, the fastest rate rises in decades sent the Nasdaq down more than 30 % and long-dated bonds down more than 20 %. Banks usually benefit at first.
steps.key: When money gets more expensive, the future is worth less.

u18l4.title: The data that moves the market

steps.title: The economic calendar
steps.body:
• **CPI/HICP:** inflation. It decides interest rates.
• **GDP:** how fast the economy is growing.
• **Jobs:** in the US, non-farm payrolls on the first Friday of each month; in Spain, the EPA (labour force survey) and registered unemployment.
• **PMI:** a monthly survey of purchasing managers. **Above 50 = expansion.** It comes out ahead of GDP.
• **Interest rate decisions** by the ECB and the Fed.

steps.title: Surprise versus expectation
steps.body:
If inflation is expected at 3 % and comes in at 3.4 %, the stock market can fall even if inflation is lower than the month before.

The price already reflects what's expected: what moves it is the **surprise**.

steps.title: Sometimes it's the other way round
steps.body: A very strong jobs figure can make the stock market fall: the market fears the central bank will keep rates high. Good for the economy isn't always good for the stock market on the day.
steps.key: The market doesn't react to whether the data is good or bad, but to whether it's better or worse than expected.

u18l5.title: Small and growth companies: what to look at

steps.title: When there's no profit
steps.body:
Many young companies **lose money** while they grow. The P/E is no use (there are no earnings), so you look at:

• **Sales growth** and whether it lasts.
• **Gross margin:** whether each sale makes money.
• **Price/sales:** market cap ÷ sales.
• **Cash and cash burn:** how many months it can last without asking for more money.

steps.title: The runway
steps.body:
**Months of cash = cash ÷ monthly cash burn.**

With €120m in the bank and €10m burned each month, it has **12 months**. If it doesn't start making money before then, it will have to **raise capital** (diluting you) or borrow.

steps.title: Many don't make it
steps.body: Small companies can multiply… or disappear. More than half of US shares since 1926 returned less than Treasury bills. And they're among the hardest hit when interest rates rise.
steps.key: With a loss-making company, the key question is whether it will start making money before it runs out of cash.

steps.title: The 10-question checklist
steps.body:
1. Do I understand how it makes money?
2. Is it growing?
3. Is it profitable (margins, ROE, ROIC)?
4. Does it generate cash?
5. Is it financially healthy (debt)?
6. Does it have a moat?
7. Who runs it?
8. Is it expensive?
9. What could go wrong?
10. What would make me sell?

steps.title: Let's practise with Inditex (2024 financial year)
steps.body:
• **Sales:** €38,632m (+7.5 %).
• **Gross margin:** 57.8 %.
• **EBITDA:** €10,728m · **EBIT:** €7,554m.
• **Net profit:** €5,866m (+9 %).
• **Net cash:** €11,495m (more cash than debt).
• **Dividend:** €1.68 per share.

It's an example to practise with, **not a recommendation**.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body:
• Profits growing but cash isn't.
• Debt growing without profits.
• Changes of auditor or chief financial officer.
• Constant capital raises.
• Dividends paid with debt.
• Executives selling lots of shares.
steps.key: If you can't explain in three sentences why you're buying a company, you're not ready to buy it yet.

u18l1-1.prompt: Match each example with its moat.
options: A social network with billions of users
The management software a whole company uses
A drug company with a patented medicine
A big retailer that buys more cheaply than anyone else
The only oil pipeline in a region
u18l1-1.explanation: The five moats from Morningstar and Pat Dorsey.

u18l1-2.prompt: What moat does a payment system have when almost every shop accepts it and almost every customer uses it?
u18l1-2.explanation: The more shops accept it, the more customers want it, and vice versa.

u18l1-3.prompt: Which signs in the numbers suggest a moat? Tick all that apply.
u18l1-3.explanation: Constant losses point to exactly the opposite.

u18l1-4.prompt: Ana is analysing a trendy café with queues out the door that made a lot of money last year. Three similar ones have just opened 50 metres away. What does she conclude about its moat?
options: The moat depends on how the place is decorated
It has a huge moat: there are queues
Its moat is weak: it's easy to copy and people are already copying it
u18l1-4.explanation: If a business makes a lot of money and is easy to copy, competition will arrive.
feedback: Without an advantage that's hard to copy, there's no moat.
Being trendy isn't a moat: if it's easy to copy, competitors arrive and share out the queues.
Exactly: without something stopping others from doing the same, high profits attract competition.

u18l1-5.prompt: Bruno finds a company with a crystal-clear moat… trading on a P/E of 90 and growing at 10 % a year. What does he bear in mind?
options: That its PEG is 9: the price already assumes a huge amount
That with a moat like that, any price is fine
That a high P/E guarantees it will keep rising
u18l1-5.explanation: A good business also needs a good price.
feedback: Exactly: 90 ÷ 10 = 9. A great business can be a bad investment if you overpay.
Microsoft had a moat in 2000 too, and anyone who bought at the peak took about 16 years to break even.
It doesn't guarantee anything; it just signals very high expectations.

u18l1-6.prompt: A company with no competitive advantage at all can keep very high margins for decades.
u18l1-6.explanation: High margins attract competitors; without a moat, they end up falling.

u18l1-7.prompt: Is it a moat or not?
options: Customers who would lose their data if they switched
An exclusive licence to run an airport
A product that's trendy this summer
u18l1-7.explanation: A moat is an advantage that's hard to copy and lasts.

u18l1-8.prompt: Quick: a messaging app becomes more valuable with every new user. What moat is that?
u18l1-8.explanation: Each user makes the product more useful for everyone else.

u18l1-9.prompt: Microsoft took about 16 years to get back to its 2000 peak. If inflation had been 2 % a year, how much purchasing power would someone who got back exactly to that price have lost? (in %)
u18l1-9.explanation: 1 ÷ 1.02¹⁶ ≈ 0.728: 27 % less purchasing power over 16 years, not counting dividends.

u18l1-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: No, brands are never a moat
Yes: if you like it, everyone does
It might have a moat, but you need to see it in its margins and ROIC, and look at the price as well
u18l1-10.explanation: Look for the moat in the numbers and don't forget the price.
feedback: Strong brands can be a very powerful moat.
Liking it is a starting point, not an analysis.
OK: liking the product doesn't tell me whether the share is expensive.
lines: I love this brand, I use it every day 😍
Does that mean it has a moat and it's a good investment?

u18l2-1.explanation: What people keep buying in a crisis is defensive; what they put off is cyclical.

u18l2-2.prompt: Match each phase of the cycle with what usually happens.
u18l2-2.explanation: And then it starts all over again.
right: Rates go up and growth slows
Low rates and the economy starts to grow

u18l2-3.prompt: First week of September 2008: the US has just taken over Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and there's talk of recession. What did the S&P 500 do in the following months?
u18l2-3.explanation: In the middle of the financial crisis, nobody knew how far the contagion to the real economy would spread. Cyclicals, like banks and industrials, were the most exposed.

u18l2-4.prompt: March 2009: unemployment is soaring and the headlines are terrible. The S&P 500 has fallen more than 50 % from its peak. What did it do next?
u18l2-4.explanation: With news that bad, almost nobody dared to make a decision. Remember that the stock market looks at what it expects months ahead, not at what's happening today.

options: A 10 % fall in the stock market
Two quarters in a row of falling GDP

u18l2-6.prompt: The stock market usually hits bottom once the economic data has already improved.
u18l2-6.explanation: It usually gets there first: in 2009 and 2020 it hit bottom while the news was still very bad.

u18l2-7.prompt: The data points to a slowdown. Pablo has almost his whole portfolio in banks, carmakers and hotels. What risk is he running?
options: He's heavily concentrated in cyclicals, which usually fall more if a recession comes
None: those sectors always go up
u18l2-7.explanation: Spreading across cyclical and defensive sectors makes you less dependent on the cycle.
feedback: Exactly: it's not about predicting the recession, but about not relying on a single kind of sector.
They do exist: food, healthcare, utilities…
They're precisely the most sensitive to the cycle: they fall more in recessions.

u18l2-8.prompt: Quick: which sector usually falls least in a recession?
u18l2-8.explanation: People keep buying food in a crisis.

u18l2-9.prompt: Which sectors are defensive? Tick all that apply.

u18l2-10.prompt: In a recession, a cyclical sector falls 40 %. How much does it then need to rise to get back to where it was?
u18l2-10.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 1.667 → +66.7 %. A defensive sector that falls 15 % only needs +17.6 %.

u18l3-1.prompt: January 2022: US inflation is at a near 40-year high and the Fed is preparing to raise rates. This is an ETF of US Treasury bonds with more than 20 years to maturity. What did it do next?
u18l3-1.explanation: Long-dated bonds are very sensitive to interest rates: the further away the money they pay, the more their value today changes when rates move.

u18l3-2.prompt: Put in order what happens when the central bank raises rates.
u18l3-2.explanation: With a lag of 12 to 24 months between the first step and the last.

u18l3-3.prompt: The ECB raises rates by more than expected. Laura has a young tech company with no profits, a bank and a 30-year bond fund. Which part usually suffers least in the short term?
u18l3-3.explanation: Rate rises mainly punish whatever depends on the distant future.
feedback: It's the most sensitive: its value depends on profits a long way off.
It's one of the things that falls most when rates go up.
Exactly: at first, banks usually earn more on their loans. Though if the economy slows sharply, they suffer too.

u18l3-4.prompt: What is the ECB's inflation target?
u18l3-4.explanation: That's why it acts when inflation drifts away from 2 %.

u18l3-5.prompt: A bond pays €20 a year forever. With rates at 2 %, it's worth 20 ÷ 0.02 = €1,000. How much would it be worth if rates rose to 4 %?
u18l3-5.explanation: 20 ÷ 0.04 = €500: rates double and the price halves. That's why the longest-dated bonds suffered so much in 2022.

u18l3-6.prompt: Rate rises usually benefit the long-dated bonds you already hold.
u18l3-6.explanation: Their price falls: new bonds pay more, so the old ones can only be sold more cheaply.

u18l3-7.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u18l3-7.explanation: As well as setting rates, central banks move the market by buying or offloading bonds.
right: What the ECB pays banks for lending it money
The central bank reduces the bonds it holds
The central bank buys bonds to inject money

u18l3-8.prompt: Quick: rates go up. Which company's shares usually suffer most?
options: Young tech company with no profits
u18l3-8.explanation: Its value depends on profits a long way off, which get discounted more heavily.

u18l3-9.prompt: In 2022, tech shares and long-dated bonds fell at the same time.
u18l3-9.explanation: The Nasdaq fell more than 30 % and long-dated bonds more than 20 %: rising rates hit both.

u18l3-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: It has no effect at all
It's usually positive, but it depends on whether it was already expected and why they're cutting
u18l3-10.explanation: Cutting rates usually helps shares and bonds, but the surprise and the reason matter.
feedback: Interest rates are the price of money: they affect everything.
Ah! If they're cutting because a crisis is coming, maybe it's not such good news.
The opposite: it usually boosts the economy and helps shares and bonds… unless it's done out of fear of a crisis.
lines: The ECB has cut interest rates 📉
Is that good or bad for the stock market?

u18l4-1.prompt: Match each indicator with what it measures.
u18l4-1.explanation: The most closely watched data on the calendar.
right: Factory and services activity, by survey
How fast the economy is growing

u18l4-3.prompt: A PMI above ____ indicates that activity is expanding.

u18l4-4.prompt: Inflation is expected at 2.8 % and comes in at 3.3 %. You have a big position in long-dated bonds. What's most likely to happen that day?
options: The bonds fall: the market now expects higher rates
u18l4-4.explanation: What counts is the gap between the figure and what was expected.
feedback: 2.8 % was expected, not 3.3 %: there's a surprise.
Exactly: an upside surprise in inflation puts pressure on bond prices.
A worse-than-expected figure pushes rate cuts further away: they would normally fall.

u18l4-5.prompt: Friday: the US jobs figure comes in far better than expected and the stock market falls. Marta doesn't get it. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The stock market always falls on Fridays
The market fears the Fed will keep rates high for longer
u18l4-5.explanation: Good for the economy isn't always good for the stock market on the day.
feedback: There's no such rule.
Exactly: good news for the economy, bad news for anyone hoping for rate cuts.
The figure is real; the market is thinking about what the Fed will do.

u18l4-6.prompt: Why is the PMI followed so closely?
options: Because it measures the price of gold
Because it comes out ahead of GDP
Because the stock exchange publishes it
u18l4-6.explanation: It's a monthly survey that arrives long before the GDP figure.

u18l4-7.prompt: The market expected one figure and got another. Positive or negative surprise for the stock market?
options: Inflation expected at 2.5 %; comes in at 3.1 %
PMI expected at 48; comes in at 51
GDP expected at +0.5 %; comes in at −0.2 %
Inflation expected at 3 %; comes in at 2.6 %
u18l4-7.explanation: Lower inflation and more activity than expected usually go down well; the opposite doesn't.

u18l4-8.prompt: The market reacts mainly to whether the figure is good or bad, not to what was expected.
u18l4-8.explanation: It reacts to the surprise: what was expected is already in the price.

u18l4-9.prompt: Which data usually moves markets most? Tick all that apply.
options: The number of visitors to a museum
Interest rate decisions by the ECB and the Fed
u18l4-9.explanation: Rates, inflation and jobs shape monetary policy.

u18l4-10.prompt: GDP was expected at +0.3 % and comes in at +0.3 %. Most likely reaction?
options: Not much: it was already priced in
u18l4-10.explanation: Without a surprise, there's not much to adjust.

u18l5-1.prompt: A company has €90m in cash and burns €7.5m a month. How many months of cash does it have?

u18l5-2.prompt: It has a market cap of €3,000m and sales of €200m a year. What is its price/sales ratio?
u18l5-2.explanation: 3,000 ÷ 200 = 15: you're paying 15 years of sales, not of profits.

u18l5-3.prompt: You own 1 million shares in a company that has 100 million (1 %). It raises capital by issuing 25 million new shares and you don't take part. What percentage do you own now?

u18l5-4.prompt: A company had sales of €50m last year and €80m this year. How much have its sales grown?

u18l5-5.prompt: Ana finds a small company growing sales by 80 %, losing money and with enough cash for 6 months. On a forum they say it's «going to 10x». What does she look at first?
options: How it's going to fund itself: a capital raise, debt or turning a profit in time
How many followers the forum has
Nothing: if it's growing that fast, it'll be fine
u18l5-5.explanation: Growing without cash is a race against the clock.
feedback: Exactly: with 6 months of cash, a capital raise that dilutes her is very likely.
Popularity doesn't pay the wages.
With 6 months of cash, the most likely thing in the short term is that it needs more money.

u18l5-6.prompt: A company keeps selling more, but its gross margin is 5 % and falling: almost everything it takes in goes on the cost of making the sale. How does it look?
options: Bad sign: growing like this doesn't bring it any closer to making money
The margin doesn't matter if sales are going up
u18l5-6.explanation: Look at whether each sale makes money, not just how many sales there are.
feedback: Growing by selling at almost no margin doesn't bring profits closer: it pushes them further away.
Exactly: growth is only worth it if each sale leaves something behind.
The margin tells you whether growth creates value or eats it up.

u18l5-7.prompt: Why is the P/E no use for a company that's losing money?
options: Because without earnings it comes out negative and makes no sense
Because it's forbidden to calculate it
Because it always comes out at 15
u18l5-7.explanation: That's why you look at sales, margins and cash.

u18l5-8.prompt: Loss-making growth companies usually suffer more when interest rates go up.
u18l5-8.explanation: Their value depends on profits a long way off, which are worth less today when rates are higher.

u18l5-9.prompt: Quick: €60m of cash and €5m burned a month. Months of cash?

u18l5-10.prompt: What's worth looking at in a young company with no profits? Tick everything useful.
options: How often it appears on social media
u18l5-10.explanation: Growth, margin and cash tell you whether the business can become profitable.

u18l6-1.prompt: Put the first five steps of the checklist in order.
options: Do I understand how it makes money?
u18l6-1.explanation: First understand the business; then its numbers.

u18l6-2.prompt: Using the Inditex figures, what was its EBIT margin (EBIT ÷ sales)? (one decimal place)
u18l6-2.explanation: 7,554 ÷ 38,632 ≈ 19.6 %: out of every €100 of sales, almost €20 of operating profit.

u18l6-3.prompt: Inditex had €11,495m of net cash. What does that tell you about its net debt/EBITDA?
options: That it's about 10 times: very worrying
That nothing can be said about it
That it's negative: it has more cash than debt
u18l6-3.explanation: With net cash, question 5 («is it financially healthy?») is quickly answered.

u18l6-4.prompt: Which are red flags? Tick all that apply.
options: Free cash flow in line with profits
u18l6-4.explanation: Cash that keeps pace with profits is a good sign.

u18l6-5.prompt: Real chart of an IBEX 35 share: 30 sessions with no name or date. Even if you'd done your 30-minute analysis, would you know what it did over the next 10?
u18l6-5.explanation: A good analysis tells you whether the business is good and whether its price is reasonable; it doesn't tell you what the price will do in two weeks.

u18l6-6.prompt: Real price of a big tech company over two months. Tap the highest point. (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · June–August 2026)
u18l6-6.explanation: A two-month high doesn't tell you whether the business is good: the checklist answers that.

u18l6-7.prompt: Inditex paid a dividend of €1.68 and its earnings per share were about €1.88. What was its approximate payout ratio?
u18l6-7.explanation: 1.68 ÷ 1.88 ≈ 89 %. It included a €0.55 special dividend; with so much net cash, a high payout ratio is easier to sustain than with debt.

u18l6-8.prompt: You've run the checklist on a company: it's growing, very profitable, generates cash, has no debt and has a strong brand. But it trades on a P/E well above its historical average. What do you conclude?
options: A safe buy: it's a great business
It's a great business, but I need to decide whether the price leaves a margin of safety
u18l6-8.explanation: A good business also needs a good price.
feedback: A great business isn't the same as a great investment: the price matters.
Nothing suggests that: it's a healthy business at a demanding price.
Exactly: question 8 («is it expensive?») carries as much weight as the others.

u18l6-9.prompt: Quick: according to your analysis, when does it make sense to sell?
options: When the investment thesis breaks down
u18l6-9.explanation: The price can fall without the business getting worse.

u18l6-10.prompt: What should a good investment thesis include? Tick everything that applies.
options: Why the price is below the value
u18l6-10.explanation: A thesis explains why the business is worth more than its price, and when you'd stop believing it.
